explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "I know your deeds; you are neither cold nor hot." Then He adds, "How I wish you were one or the other!" (Revelation 3:15)

Nope, friend, but I see why you'd hope so. Jesus says, "you are neither cold nor hot." He doesn't say they're hot. He says, "How I wish you were one or the other!" so the church in Laodicea sits in the middle.

Not quite, baker. Jesus says they're "…neither cold nor hot." Cold isn't the answer, because He puts them right in the middle. Then He says, "How I wish you were one or the other!" so He wants them to be one of the two, not stuck between.

explanations.answer: Vomit them out of His mouth
explanations.explanation: Yep. That's a strong picture. He says, "So because you are lukewarm—neither hot nor cold—I am about to vomit you out of My mouth!" I think this is one of those lines you read once and sit with for a minute. It's heavy, and it comes right after He says He wishes they were hot or cold.

Close, but that's not what He says. Jesus says He is about to vomit them out of His mouth. A shut door doesn't show up in this part at all. A few verses later it's the opposite, because He stands at the door and knocks (Revelation 3:20).

Not in this verse, baker. Here Jesus says, "…I am about to vomit you out of My mouth!" He says that because they're lukewarm, neither hot nor cold. Blotting out a name is a different picture than the one He uses for Laodicea.

Right, friend. Laodicea says, "I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing." Jesus answers that they don't realize they are "…wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked." That's a big gap between what they say about themselves and what He sees.

Good guess, but hungry isn't on His list. Jesus says they don't realize they are "…wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked." Poor is the one that answers their boast about being rich. Hungry never comes up.

Not this time, baker. Jesus never says alone in this part. He says they don't realize they are "…wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked." Alone isn't the word, and later in this letter He's the One standing at a door and knocking.

You got it, baker. Jesus says, "I counsel you to buy from Me gold refined by fire so that you may become rich…" They said they were rich, and He tells them how to actually become rich. And notice who they're buying it from. It's from Him.

Nice try, friend, but silver isn't in this verse. Jesus counsels them to buy "…gold refined by fire so that you may become rich…" He doesn't mention the temple at all. And they buy it from Him, not from anywhere else.

A pearl of great value shows up in one of Jesus' parables (Matthew 13:46), but not here. In this letter He counsels them to buy "…gold refined by fire so that you may become rich…" So the shopping list has gold on it, not pearls.

That's the one. Jesus counsels them to buy "…white garments so that you may be clothed and your shameful nakedness not exposed…" They were called naked a verse earlier. Now He points them to the clothes.

Sounds fancy, but no crown in this verse. Jesus counsels them to buy white garments "…so that you may be clothed and your shameful nakedness not exposed…" The garments are for covering them. Clothed is the word.
Not praised, baker. The verse says the white garments are "…so that you may be clothed and your shameful nakedness not exposed…" Nobody's handing out applause here. It's about covering them up.
True, friend. Jesus says they are "blind," and then counsels them to buy "…salve to anoint your eyes so that you may see." He doesn't just name the problem. He offers the fix.
It's actually true, baker. Jesus says Laodicea is "blind," and then counsels them to buy "…salve to anoint your eyes so that you may see." So He doesn't leave them stuck. He points them to the fix.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, "Those I love I rebuke and discipline." That changes how the hard words sound. He's saying them to people He loves, and they're not coming from a stranger.
Not quite, friend. Doubt isn't what He names. Jesus says, "Those I love I rebuke and discipline." So the rebuke comes along with love.
Close to the mood, but that's not what He says. Jesus says, "Those I love I rebuke and discipline." Forgetting Him isn't mentioned in this verse. Love is who He names.

True, baker. Right after He says He rebukes and disciplines those He loves, Jesus says, "Therefore be earnest and repent." It's a direct word to the church in Laodicea. And it follows right behind the love.
It's true, friend. Jesus says, "Therefore be earnest and repent." He says it right after, "Those I love I rebuke and discipline." So the call to repent is part of what He tells Laodicea.
Not this time, baker. Jesus says, "If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in…" He says anyone, and He doesn't say only leaders. So it's anyone who hears Him and opens the door.

Right. Jesus says, "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me." The word is anyone. He doesn't limit it to the leaders.

explanations.answer: Come in and dine with them
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Jesus says, "…I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me." He comes inside to share a meal with them. I love that, because a meal is where people really stay a while.

explanations.answer: Talk with them at the door
explanations.explanation: Close, baker, but He goes further than the doorway. Jesus says, "…I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me." He comes inside. Dining together is the promise.

explanations.answer: Walk with them down the road
explanations.explanation: Not here, friend. This verse has no road at all. Jesus says, "…I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me." So the scene stays at the door and then moves inside, to a meal.

explanations.answer: The right to sit with Him on His throne
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne, just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne." That is a BIG promise. And it comes to a church He just called lukewarm.

explanations.answer: A home inside the new Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That one doesn't show up here, friend. Jesus speaks of the new Jerusalem in His letter to the church in Philadelphia (Revelation 3:12). Here, to the one who overcomes, He says, "…I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne…" So the throne is the promise in this letter.

explanations.answer: A crown of twelve shining stars
explanations.explanation: Twelve stars do show up in Revelation, on a woman's crown (Revelation 12:1), but that's a different scene. In this letter Jesus promises the one who overcomes "…the right to sit with Me on My throne…" It's even compared to how He sat down with His Father on His throne. No stars in this one, baker.
